articles.text: The settlers on the Crow Creek reservation seem to be confident that they will not be disturbed for some time and that they can bring their case to the attention of Crongress before Cleveland enforces his order for the reservation to be vacated.
articles.summary: Settlers on the Crow Creek reservation expect to bring their case to Congress before Cleveland's order to vacate is enforced.

articles.text: At the latest account, Gen. Crook had not made much headway in his war with the southern Indians and the settlers were beginning to organize for their own protection. When will the people at large and the general government learn the true definition of a good Indian?
articles.summary: Editorial remark on Gen. Crook's slow progress against the southern Apaches and settlers organizing for self-protection.

articles.text: Fred. Willard, our new stock inspector, returned Monday evening from Fargo, where he had gone to receive his commission as deputy U. S. Marshal. He says he hopes there will be no occasion for his services in the latter capacity. His wife will be here in a few weeks.
articles.summary: Fred Willard, the new stock inspector, returned from Fargo with his commission as deputy U.S. marshal.

articles.text: Russia is still continuing her warlike preparations and under the surface there is trouble in European politics. It has long been known that Lord Salisbury desired to form an offensive alliance with Germany against Russia and this, in connection with Russia's war preparations creates a very uneasy feeling. We still live in hopes of a European war.
articles.summary: Editorial comment on Russian war preparations and European tension.

articles.text: The trial of Mrs. Yseult Dudley, for shooting O'Donovan Rossa, began yesterday in New York. She proved herself to be a regular vixen, constantly interrupting Rossa's testimony to cast slurs upon him and his evidence. She is doubtless trying the insanity dodge. Although public feeling is in her favor she will not help her case any by her present course.
articles.summary: Editorial comment on the New York trial of Yseult Dudley for shooting O'Donovan Rossa.

articles.text: It is a burning disgrace that even after the arrival of Bartholdi's statue of "Liberty enlightening the world," there has not been money enough raised to build the pedestal. France's generosity in presenting this gift is in striking contrast to the delay of the United States in finding it a resting place. As soon as Congress meets, it should solve the difficulty by appropriating a sufficient sum to cover the present shortage.
articles.summary: Editorial urging Congress to fund the pedestal for Bartholdi's Statue of Liberty.

articles.text: That General Grant is dying, seems now to admit of no doubt. The cancerous sore is now involving his jugular vein and he writes all communications to his physicians and attendants. Monday, he wrote on his writing tab: "Do as I do. I give myself not the least concern. If I knew that the end would be to-morrow, I would try and get rest in the meantime. As long as there's no no progress, there's hope." It seems that even to the end he will keep up the same stoical coolness that has been his marked characteristic.
articles.summary: Editorial on General Grant's terminal illness, quoting a note he wrote Monday.

articles.text: The division idea is again being forced on the people by newspapers whose editors see some official pap in the dim future. It is needless to hope for a time when the press and political leaders of Dakota will unite for admission of Dakota as a whole, to make in the future one of the best of states. The animus of the whole division movement arises from the desire of Dakota's numerous political aspirants to double the number of state offices and thereby be more certain of an office for themselves. We have not; do not and never will uphold the action o these politicians in trying to increase the burden of taxation for their own benefit. Spot a divisionist as an axe-grinder every time.
articles.summary: Editorial opposing division of Dakota Territory and favoring admission as a whole.

articles.text: We notice that it is the prevalent opinion that the recent assessment of Billings county by Stark county is for the purpose of levying a territorial tax. How this impression has gained ground is a mystery, as the assessment is strictly and solely a county tax and is entirely for the use and behoof of Stark county. It seems that the idea of this being a territorial tax has come from Stark county and if so, goes to prove what we thoroughly believe, that the law empowering senior counties to tax junior counties is unconstitutional. All debts contracted by senior counties to pay expenses of unorganized counties are finally paid by the territory. Where then is the justice of the senior counties being twice paid for those expenses? It would be a good plan to have this matter carefully considered by our citizens, and if deemed advisable, to make a test case and decide the constitutionality of the law. In any event, every one who pays taxes to Stark county should do so under protest so that in case a test case should be tried it will be easier to get our money returned.
articles.summary: Editorial arguing that Stark county's assessment of Billings county is a county, not territorial, tax, questioning its constitutionality and urging taxpayers to pay under protest.

articles.text: The Chicago cattle market as will be seen by our report, shows an upward tendency on fair to prime classes of cattle, of 20 @ 35c. Texas cattle advanced 10 @ 15c. articles.text: Gen. Brisbin recently wrote an article for the Salt Lake Tribune, the substance of which should be deeply engraved in every cow-man's heart. It costs no more on the range to take care of or raise a hundred dollar animal than it does one worth forty dollars. Except for the original cost the profit is vastly on the side of the man who raises high-grade or full-blooded cattle.
articles.summary: Endorses Gen. Brisbin's argument for raising high-grade cattle.

articles.text: The second annual round-up of this district came to a close at Mingusville Monday morning. The estimate of the calf crop at sixty per cent. is, if anything, too high. On the whole, the round-up was a success, although, on account of the difficulty of working the Bad Lands it is impossible to get the satisfactory results obtainable on more open ranges.
articles.summary: The district's second annual round-up closed at Mingusville Monday morning; the calf crop is estimated at under sixty per cent.

articles.text: The Texas and New Mexico round-ups are strictly enforcing their rules forbidding the carrying of six-shooters. A cow-boy near Springer, N. M. recently had one taken from him and was fined $25 besides. If this rule can be made to work in old cattle countries it certainly can here. If it is necessary there, it is necessary here. Who of our western readers is there that does not know of one or more instances where serious or fatal accidents would not have happened if the six-shooter had been prohibited? Does the satisfaction of carrying six-shooters pay for the loss of life and suffering occasioned by them? We certainly think not and will hail the day when the habitual carrying of six-shooters is ended. There are occasions when it is necessary to carry revolvers but these do not come as often as every waking hour for three hundred and sixty-five days in the year.
articles.summary: Editorial endorsing Texas and New Mexico round-up rules against carrying six-shooters and urging the same locally.

articles.text: There are Percherons, so-called, which are not Percherons, any more than Pennsylvanians are Virginians; but they are both French, as these are Americans. Perche is an ancient province of France, and lies south of Normandy, adjoining its southwestern border. Perche has long been known for its splendid breed of horses, which have been reared with much care and jealousy, and which date back in breeding to Arabian blood. Normandy has also its breed of horses, equally ancient but coarser and heavier; they were used a thousand years ago in war when an enormous weight of steel armour was borne, both by the rider and the horse. To bear the burden, and to ride down an opponent by mere force of shock, very heavy horses were required, rather than more active ones, and the Norman horses thus became, as they are still, they heaviest race known. The Percherons, on the other hand, were used for carriages, and are now the stage, omnibus and diligence horses of the country, able to trot with ease ten miles an hour, with a heavy vehicle behind them. These are consequently more finely built, have harder and finer bone, and while quite heavy, look lighter than they really are, because of their fine proportions, due to their Arabian ancestry.—[American Agriculturist.
articles.summary: Clipping from the American Agriculturist on the origins of Percheron and Norman horses.

articles.headline: THE LOST CABIN GOLD MINES.
articles.text:
THE LOST CABIN GOLD MINES.

By J. S. WARN.

After a while things quieted down and by a good deal of talking the excited men were shown the folly of their suspicions and that Hulbert could not possibly have gained anything by lying to them. In the morning we made an early start and after two days' hard drive we found Bozeman camped on the Big Horn river below the canon. Hulbert thought when he first saw the Big Horn that it was the Yellowstone and he rode up and down the train excitedly declaring that now he was certain of the location of the mines. Again was he doomed to disappointment but he still insisted that he would reach the mines all right when we could find the Yellowstone. He knew the country there and could reach the mines without fail. But all except a few of the people in the train had entirely lost faith in Hulbert and could not be aroused from their discouragement. A discouraged tendefoot is the most miserable work of God. He is a worse failure than old Sitting Bull would be as a Prohibition candidate for the presidency.

Early in the morning we made a fresh start and crossed the river. What a hard job it was, only the old timers who have had to find their own roads, build their own bridges and work their way first in new countries can imagine. After an all days' job we finally crossed, with the loss of two wagons and their contents and went into camp.

The next day, all of the two trains pulled out for the Yellowstone. In time we reached it after very severe labor, we having to make roads all the way. When we finally reached the banks of the Yellowstone we found ourselves in a beautiful grove near some high bluffs. All that wanted to, went fishing and never was sport better rewardeds as the river was full of trout. From this point Capt. Hulbert could see down the river for a long way and he declared that this was the country he had been in. He said that he had been at this very spot and that he could easily find his way to the mines. We hunted up Bozeman and talked the matter over with him and all the leading men of both trains. We tried to stir up a friendly feeling and worked hard to get at least a part of the train to keep on in the search. Hulbert was positive in his statements that he could go to the mines. He said that a short distance down the river was the island on which he had camped, that there was a good crossing here and a good place to get out of the valley. However, it was impossible to interest enough now to even protect ourselves from the Indians. As they were on the war-path big at this time, it wouldn't have done for a small body of men to start out alone. After trying our best we had to give up our persuasions. For the present the chicken-hearted pilgrims were determined to go to Virginia City. They finally did and found every claim taken, clear up and down the gulch and a claim owner wouldn't look at a tenderfoot. For my part, I would have been glad to see every one of them starve.

Those who were willing to take chances of going in as soon as the Indians were again at peace, formed themselves into a company and took each others' addresses, both in the states and Montana, for the purpose of going to these mines, as we had the utmost confidence in the stories Capt. Hulbert told.

I saw Capt. Hulbert in Virginia City in the fall of '64. He was still engaged in trying to get men to go with him but he was always unsuccessful. I saw Bozeman in the fall of '66. I was going to the states in the winter in a mackinaw boat and took his wife with me to Omaha. That is the last I have seen of them. Bozeman was killed by the Indians down in the Yellowstone country and I have always thought he was going in search of the Hulbert mines.

For my part, I have by no means given up hope of finding the mines and expect soon to start in search of them. I am as certain they exist as decribed by Hulbert, as I am of any [uncertainty?]. The Lost Cabin mine will yet be found and richly repay the finder.

(Concluded.)
articles.summary: Final installment of J. S. Warn's reminiscence of the 1860s search with Capt. Hulbert and John Bozeman for the Lost Cabin gold mine in the Big Horn and Yellowstone country.

articles.headline: Daring Exploit of Cowboys.
articles.text:
Daring Exploit of Cowboys.

A traveler on the Northern Pacific reports the following thrilling incident: When the train stopped at Medora, Montana, the headquarters of the Marquis de Mores and Theodore Roosevelt, some ten or a dozen cowboys, mounted on their typical horses of the plains, were cutting all kinds of capers and giving a sort of free show, for the edification and amusement of the citizens and passengers. They were putting the horses through reckless evolutions and maneuvers, giving an exhibition of equestrianism that astonished the tenderfeet on board the train. The boys had just come in from a round-up, and were flush with money and considerably flushed with Dakota tanglefoot. The railroad bridge, which spans the Little Missoury river at this point, is at least 100 feet above the surface of the water. To enable footmen to cross a narrow plank walk—not more than two feet wide—is laid along on the ties, from shore to shore, in the center of the bridge. It requires steady nerve for a man to make the trip successfully, without losing his balance and falling through between the ties into the river far below, which, of course would mean certain death. Two of the cowboys—more reckless than their companions—rode their horses upon the track at a rapid gait, and then, in single file, dashed on to the bridge and made for the other side, flying along on the narrow plank walk just as if they were racing across the prairie after an obstreperous bovine.

The spectators were thrilled with horror, and expected to see the two daring men dashed to death at every jump the horses made. The riders yelled vociferously, and rode with the same easy confidence they always display when at home upon the plains.
articles.summary: Syndicated (ready-print) item in which a Northern Pacific traveler describes cowboys at Medora, "the headquarters of the Marquis de Mores and Theodore Roosevelt," riding across the railroad bridge plank walk; it begins at the foot of column 4 and continues at the top of column 5.

articles.text: Johnny G. may be an expert at herding steers but when he attempts to herd a team down a twenty-foot wash-out, his last Sundays experience showed that his grand and lofty tumbling education had been neglected.
articles.summary: Joke about Johnny G.'s tumble driving a team down a wash-out last Sunday.

articles.text: John Warn has bought the Commercial house in Glendive, is now refitting it and expects to open July 4. His friends here wish him the best of success. The last of his interesting articles on the Lost Cabin gold mine appears in to-day's issue.
articles.summary: John Warn bought the Commercial house in Glendive; his last Lost Cabin article appears in this issue.

articles.text: The most severe storm of the season occured last Friday afternoon. During its continuance a bolt of lightning struck the Metropolitan hotel, not however, doing serious damage. Several persons standing in the office received shocks.
articles.summary: Lightning struck the Metropolitan hotel during the season's worst storm last Friday.

articles.text: Two men were arrested this morning by Fred. Willard. At first they did not give a satisfactory account of themselves, but it is presumed now that they are all right.
articles.summary: Fred. Willard arrested two men who later appeared to be all right.

articles.text: Joe McCoul had a serious accident Tuesday at Van Eeghan's Garner creek ranch. He was hauling a load of posts with a gentle horse and a broncho when the latter started to run away, throwing Joe off the load, breaking his leg and spraining his ankle. He was brought to town and is now at the Pyramid Park hotel. Dr. Duncan was called from Glendive and states that the fracture is not serious but the sprain is liable to cause trouble.
articles.summary: Joe McCoul broke his leg in a runaway at Van Eeghan's Garner creek ranch and is at the Pyramid Park hotel.

articles.text: Again we weep. Our proud position as fighting editor will be occupied by us no more forever. Our heavy-weight assistant who at train time makes the air musical and the pilgrims' eyes bug out by his blood-curdling way of shouting: "B-a-d L-a-n-d-s C-o-w B-o-y" has usurped our prerogative, so to speak. A callow news-boy who objected to the aforesaid heavy-weight assistant's presence on the train is now mourning his rash objection. So, we might add, are his eyes. The above should be a warning both now and forever to all news-boys not to interfere with our b-a-d man.
articles.summary: Humorous note that the Cow Boy's heavy-weight train-time newsboy thrashed a rival newsboy on the train.

articles.text: A little breeze of excitement was created this morning by the barber shop catching afire. No damage of any amount was done but the cause of the fire deserves comment. It was owing to a stove-pipe being used in place of a brick chimney. There are a number of pipes in town used in the same way. Even with secure fastenings, this is an extremely dangerous expedient, certainly a false economy. Persons having such chimneys should immediately see to it that brick ones take their place. The cost is slight in comparison to the additional safety secured.
articles.summary: The barber shop caught fire from a stove-pipe chimney; little damage.

articles.text: The meeting to get up a programme for the 4th. of July sports met according to call in the skating rink last Friday evening. J. C. Fisher was elected chairman and A. T. Packard stated that the object of the meeting was to informally discuss a programme of races and contests for the 4th. and moved that a committee of five be appointed to take charge of affairs. Bob. Roberts moved to amend by placing the name of the original mover at the head of the committee. The following committee was then elected: A. T. Packard, Bob. Roberts, E. Deffebach, John Goodall and Vic Smith. It was decided to make the principal event a six hundred yards' cow-horse race, with prizes of $25, $15 and $10. This race is open to cow-horses only or to those that are not considered or known to be fast horses. Besides this race, there are on the programme a free-for-all three hundred yards' horse race, with prizes of $15 and $10, a slow mule race, a hundred yards' dash foot race, a fat men's race, a rifle contest and other races contests which will be arranged on the ground. The base-ball will be in the forenoon, the rifle contest at one o'clock. The other contests will follow. Entries in any of the contests can be made with any of the committee.
articles.summary: A meeting at the skating rink named a committee and set a Fourth of July programme of horse, mule and foot races, a rifle contest and base-ball.
